opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it can take us a very long way, further than most people expect. If you look at the history of science, the big leaps have come from finding a small number of regularities that explain a huge range of phenomena. Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations, the standard model: a handful of equations, and they cover an enormous swath of reality. I don't see why intelligence should be fundamentally different. The world we live in isn't arbitrary. It has structure, and that structure is what makes learning possible in the first place. If the world were random, no amount of data would help you.

So the question is, what are those regularities? I'd point to a few. Compositionality: the world is made of parts, which are made of parts, and so on. Symmetry: things stay the same under certain transformations, which is why convolutional networks work, because a cat is still a cat when you shift it a few pixels. Locality: most things interact mainly with things nearby, in space, in time, or in some more abstract sense. And then there's uncertainty, because the world is noisy and you have to reason probabilistically about it. If you get those few things right and build them into your learner, you get an enormous amount of leverage.

That's really the idea behind what I've called the Master Algorithm. Each of the major schools of machine learning, the symbolists, the connectionists, the Bayesians, the evolutionaries, the analogizers, has latched onto one piece of the puzzle. Logic gives you compositionality, probability gives you uncertainty, neural networks give you powerful continuous representations and gradient-based learning, and so forth. None of them alone is enough, but I believe a unified learner that combines them could, in principle, learn anything that can be learned from data.

Now, the caveat. A small set of regularities doesn't mean a small amount of knowledge. The laws of physics are simple, but chemistry and biology are still very complicated, because the simple laws play out in a rich world with a lot of contingent detail. So the regularities give you the framework, the inductive bias, and then you still need data to fill in the specifics. What they buy you is enormous efficiency. Today's large models are compensating for a lack of the right biases with brute force: astronomical amounts of data and compute. A child doesn't need to read the whole internet to learn language. That tells me we're missing some of the fundamental regularities, and finding them is where a lot of the next progress is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response compares a small set of regularities to the Standard Model’s ability to cover a broad range of phenomena, then says intelligence should not be fundamentally different.

r002.rationale: It says the regularities could take AI “a very long way,” but gives no estimate of roughly 80%.

fable-5.1.text:
Pretty far. Farther than most people in the field are comfortable admitting, actually. The whole premise of The Master Algorithm is that there's a single learner that could, in principle, derive all knowledge from data, and I still believe that. The reason I believe it isn't mysticism, it's that it's already happened once. Evolution is a learner, and it produced the brain. The brain is a learner, and it produced science. Those are universal learners in a meaningful sense, and neither of them is a billion special cases. They're a small number of mechanisms applied relentlessly.

Now, what does "fundamental regularity" mean here? I'd say there are maybe five big ideas that keep showing up. You have the symbolist notion that knowledge is composable, that you can take pieces and recombine them. You have the connectionist idea that learning is credit assignment through a network. You have the evolutionary idea of variation and selection. You have the Bayesian idea that everything is uncertainty and you update on evidence. And you have the analogizer's idea that similar things behave similarly. Each of these camps thinks it has the answer, and each of them is wrong in the same way, which is that they've captured one regularity and declared victory.

What I find striking about the last few years is that deep learning has shown just how much you can get from almost nothing. A transformer is a very small amount of inductive bias. Attention is basically a soft form of similarity, so it's an analogizer at heart, and then you have composition through layers and credit assignment through backprop. That's it. And from that tiny set of regularities plus enormous amounts of data, you get systems that write code and pass the bar exam. If you'd told people in 2010 that this would come from such a thin set of priors, they'd have laughed at you.

But here's where I get off the hype train. The fact that a small set of regularities takes you far doesn't mean the current small set is the right one. Deep learning is extraordinarily data hungry precisely because its regularities are too weak. A child learns a word from one or two examples. An LLM needs to see it thousands of times. That gap is telling you something is missing. My bet is that what's missing is explicit composition and explicit reasoning about structure, the symbolist contribution, which the deep learning community spent a decade pretending it didn't need and is now quietly reinventing under other names.

So my honest answer is: a small set of fundamental regularities can take you all the way, but only if it's the right small set, and we don't have it yet. We have a few of the pieces working beautifully and a few of them bolted on awkwardly. The unification is the real research problem, and I think it's much closer than the people who say "just scale" believe, and much farther than the people who say "AGI next year" believe.

astra-6.text:
I think potentially a very long way. The history of science is full of cases where an enormous variety of phenomena turns out to follow from a few relatively simple principles. The interesting question is whether learning has that same character: can a small set of mechanisms account for the many different things we associate with intelligence?

My suspicion is that they can. You don’t necessarily need a separate fundamental algorithm for vision, language, reasoning, and so on. But that doesn’t mean a few principles make all the engineering disappear. Evolution is a simple idea; the organisms it produces are extraordinarily complex. Likewise, a fairly simple learning process, interacting with enough data and the right environment, could produce very complex intelligence.

So I would distinguish between the simplicity of the underlying principles and the complexity of what has to be learned. A small set of regularities might take us very far on the first, while leaving an enormous amount of work on the second.

sol-6.1.text:
I think potentially very far. The astonishing thing about science is how much complexity you can explain with a small number of principles. Evolution is a good example: a relatively simple process produces this extraordinary diversity of organisms. So the complexity of intelligence doesn’t necessarily imply that the principles underlying it have to be equally complex.

In machine learning, we already see the same algorithms working across very different domains. That suggests there are general principles of learning that we can discover and exploit. But the principles alone aren’t enough. You also need data, computation, and interaction with the world. A compact learning algorithm could generate very sophisticated intelligence because the complexity comes partly from what it learns, rather than everything having to be built into it.

The open question is whether we have the right principles yet. I think we should be ambitious about finding them, while being careful not to mistake success on a particular set of tasks for having solved intelligence.
